name: Taniwha
description: Supernatural beings in Māori tradition that inhabit deep pools, rivers, harbours, caves, and dangerous coastal waters of Aotearoa (New Zealand), acting as both guardians (kaitiaki) and monstrous threats.
full_description: Taniwha are large supernatural beings in Māori mythology, associated above all with water — deep river pools, lakes, harbours, caves, and stretches of coast with dangerous currents or reefs. They take many forms, including reptilian and dragon-like creatures, sharks, whales, geckos, and even floating logs. Many iwi (tribes) and hapū (sub-tribes) have a specific named taniwha as a kaitiaki (guardian) of a particular place, often understood as a tīpuna (ancestor) accompanying or descended from a founding canoe. Taniwha can be benevolent — warning of approaching enemies, rescuing people from drowning, or marking the proper boundaries of tapu (sacred restriction) — or destructive, taking those who transgress local laws or trespass on sacred waters. The word taniwha itself is cognate with terms for large sharks across the wider Polynesian language family (Proto-Oceanic *tanifa). Taniwha remain an active part of Māori cultural and political life: in 2002, Ngāti Naho successfully argued for the rerouting of a section of New Zealand State Highway 1 to protect the habitat of the taniwha Karutahi.

aliases.name: *tanifa
aliases.meaning: reconstructed ancestor of the word, referring to a dangerous shark species

aliases.name: Tanifa / Tanifoa
aliases.meaning: cognate terms for large or dangerous sharks

origin: Taniwha are particular to Aotearoa (New Zealand), with cognate water beings throughout Polynesia.

etymology.origin: Polynesian; reconstructed Proto-Oceanic *tanifa, with cognates in Tongan, Samoan, and other Polynesian languages referring to dangerous sharks or sea creatures.
etymology.meaning: Originally, a name for a particular dangerous shark species; in Māori usage extended to powerful supernatural water beings.
etymology.first_use: Inherited from Proto-Polynesian; attested in early 19th-century European-language accounts of Māori tradition.

timeline.event: Sir George Grey publishes 'Polynesian Mythology', recording multiple taniwha narratives
timeline.significance: Major early European-language compilation of Māori tradition

timeline.event: John White publishes 'The Ancient History of the Maori', collecting numerous taniwha references across iwi
timeline.source: White, J. (1887), Ancient History of the Maori

timeline.event: Ngāti Naho successfully petitions Transit New Zealand to reroute a section of State Highway 1 around the lair of the taniwha Karutahi in the Waikato
timeline.significance: Demonstrates living legal/political relevance of taniwha tradition

related.name: Nāga
related.description: South and Southeast Asian serpent water spirits

cultural_notes: Taniwha are widely understood by Māori as real guardians of place, deserving of respect and ritual acknowledgement. Disregard for a taniwha's territory is held to invite misfortune.
